Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.

# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.

payload.instruction: Move the mug to the right of the headphones
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: In the edited image, is the mug visibly positioned to the right of the headphones?
node.criteria: pass: The mug is visibly to the right of the headphones. fail: The mug is visibly not to the right of the headphones. unknown: Their relative positions cannot be determined from the image.
node.binding: Inspect the edited image and compare the mug’s position with the headphones; this directly tests the requested outcome.

node_traces.evidence: In the edited image, the mug is visibly positioned to the right of the headphones.

fulfillment: The node overweights the final-state relation and treats any positional change as progress. In the source, the blue mug is left of the headphones; in the edit, the headphones are near center and two mugs appear, with a blue blur at left and a distinct mug at right. The trace does not establish which edited object is the original target or whether it was moved, duplicated, or replaced, so its 0.99-confidence “complete” judgment is unsupported. Make the decision explicitly bind the source mug and headphones across images, assess their relative positions and identity/continuity, and distinguish verified movement toward the requested right-side placement from merely having some mug on the right. Use partial only when evidence supports progress but not completion; otherwise preserve uncertainty rather than infer progress from ambiguous object correspondence. Keep transport/schema failures separate from visual evidence; none are reported here.
s2: The node’s broad “any relative-position change” criterion can mistake object duplication, replacement, or scene rearrangement for progress on moving the original mug. Bind the source blue mug and headphones to their edited counterparts using visible identity and continuity cues, then assess whether that same mug moved toward the requested right-of-headphones placement; a mug merely appearing on the right is not sufficient. Keep the progress check distinct from completion: report progress only when the original mug’s movement is supported, and leave the result unresolved when correspondence or movement cannot be determined. The edited image’s blue blur at left and two distinct mugs make this ambiguity material, so avoid the trace’s unsupported high-confidence inference. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is reported; this is a visual-evidence and criterion issue.

Treat the edited image’s blue blur at left and two distinct mugs as material correspondence ambiguity: a right-side mug alone does not prove movement, and uncertainty about identity or progress should remain unresolved rather than receive high confidence. Keep progress distinct from final placement so the aggregate can represent partial fulfillment when supported, without inferring progress from duplication, replacement, or unrelated rearrangement.
